question: Upper winds above the friction layer are produced by:

options.text: The same balance of forces as the gradient wind
Surface friction acting through the whole troposphere
Convection currents rising from the heated surface
The rotation of the jet stream around the pole alone

explanation: Above the friction layer, winds follow the pressure (contour) pattern under the same balance of forces as the gradient wind.

question: For the same pressure gradient, upper winds are generally stronger than winds near the surface because:

options.text: The pressure gradient always reverses with height above the surface
Friction increases with height, which speeds up the flow above it
The Coriolis force increases with height, accelerating the wind
Air density is lower, and geostrophic speed varies inversely with density

explanation: V = PGF / (2Ωρ sin(latitude)). At about 20 000 ft, where density is roughly half its surface value, the same gradient gives about twice the wind speed.

question: A constant-pressure (contour) chart shows:

options.text: The pressure found at a fixed height above MSL across the chart area
Lines of equal temperature at the surface
The heights above MSL at which a particular pressure is found
Lines of equal wind speed at a fixed height

explanation: For example, a 500 hPa chart is drawn with contours showing how high above MSL the 500 hPa surface lies at each point.

question: On a contour chart, contour lines are also called:

options.text: Isobars
Isohypses
Isotachs
Isotherms

explanation: Isohypses are lines of equal height. Isotachs join points of equal wind speed and isotherms points of equal temperature.

question: On a 500 hPa contour chart, an area of high contour values indicates:

options.text: An area of very cold air in the lower troposphere
Low pressure aloft, where the 500 hPa surface lies far above MSL
Strong winds blowing directly across the contour lines
High pressure aloft, where the 500 hPa surface lies far above MSL

explanation: Where the pressure surface is high above sea level, the pressure at any given height is high. High contours correspond to upper ridges and highs.

question: On a contour chart in the Northern Hemisphere, the wind at that pressure level blows:

options.text: At about 30° to the contours, towards the lower values
Parallel to the contours, with lower values on the right (back to the wind)
Parallel to the contours, with lower values on the left (back to the wind)
Across the contours, from high values towards low values

explanation: Contours behave like isobars: the wind follows them, Buys Ballot's law applies, and closer spacing means a stronger wind.

question: Closely spaced contours on a 300 hPa chart indicate:

options.text: Light winds at about FL300
Strong winds at about FL300
A col at about FL300
High temperatures at about FL300

explanation: Close contours mean a steep slope of the pressure surface and therefore a strong pressure gradient and strong winds at that level.

question: Isotachs are lines joining places of equal:

options.text: Wind speed
Pressure
Temperature
Height of a pressure level

explanation: Isotachs are drawn on upper-air charts to show wind speed patterns, especially around jet streams.

question: The approximate flight level for which a 250 hPa chart is used is:

options.text: FL300
FL240
FL390
FL340

question: The approximate flight level for which a 400 hPa chart is used is:

options.text: FL180
FL300
FL240
FL140

explanation: In the ISA the 400 hPa level is at about 23 600 ft, so it is paired with FL240.

question: The approximate flight level for which a 150 hPa chart is used is:

options.text: FL450
FL530
FL340
FL390

explanation: In the ISA, 150 hPa lies at about 44 600 ft, so it serves flight around FL450.

question: The pressure pattern at upper levels is largely determined by:

options.text: The speed of the surface wind
The mean temperature of the air columns below
The amount of cloud cover present
The size of the diurnal pressure variation

explanation: Pressure falls more slowly with height in warm air than in cold air, so high levels have relatively high pressure over warm columns and low pressure over cold columns.

question: The thermal wind is:

options.text: The vector difference between the winds at two levels
The circulation associated with a thermal low in summer
The light wind blowing up a sunny slope by day
The surface wind caused by daytime heating of the land

explanation: The change in wind with height is the thermal wind. It blows parallel to the isotherms (or thickness lines) of the layer, with cold air on the left in the Northern Hemisphere.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere, the thermal wind blows parallel to the mean isotherms with:

options.text: Cold air on the right
Warm air on the left
Cold air on the left
Cold air ahead

explanation: Buys Ballot's law extends to temperature: with your back to the thermal wind in the Northern Hemisphere, low temperature, low pressure aloft and low contour heights are on the left.

question: The extended form of Buys Ballot's law for upper winds says that, with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, the following are on your left:

options.text: High pressure, low temperature and high contour heights
Low pressure, high temperature and low contour heights
High pressure, high temperature and high contour heights
Low pressure, low temperature and low contour heights

explanation: Upper-level low pressure, low contour heights and the cold air mass all lie on the left. In the Southern Hemisphere they are on the right.

question: Because air is generally colder towards the poles, upper winds in both hemispheres tend to be:

options.text: Easterly
Westerly
Southerly
Northerly

explanation: With cold air poleward, the thermal wind blows from west to east in both hemispheres (cold on the left in the north, on the right in the south). Upper easterlies occur only in special cases such as the tropical easterly jet.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere, the surface wind is southerly and the temperature decreases northwards, with isotherms running east–west. With height, the wind will:

options.text: Back towards easterly and increase
Veer towards westerly and increase
Back towards easterly and decrease
Remain southerly and decrease

explanation: The thermal wind is westerly (cold to the north, on the left of a westerly). Adding a westerly component to a southerly wind turns it clockwise (veers) and, higher up, the westerly component dominates.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere a wind that veers with height through a layer indicates:

options.text: A thermal low at the surface
No temperature advection
Cold air advection in that layer
Warm air advection in that layer

explanation: A veering wind with height means the wind is blowing from the warmer towards the colder side of the thermal gradient, bringing warmer air. Backing with height indicates cold advection.

question: Thickness charts show:

options.text: The vertical distance between two pressure levels, a measure of the layer's mean temperature
The thickness of the tropopause layer, measured in kilometres
The thickness of cloud layers, measured from base to top in hundreds of feet
The depth of the friction layer, measured from the surface to the gradient-wind level

explanation: A warm layer is thick and a cold layer thin, so thickness lines act as mean isotherms. The thermal wind blows parallel to them.

question: High thickness values between 1000 hPa and 500 hPa indicate:

options.text: Strong surface winds
A relatively cold air column
A relatively warm air column
A deep layer of fog

explanation: Warm air expands, increasing the distance between the two pressure surfaces.

question: A jet stream is defined as a narrow, fast current of air, usually near the tropopause, with a speed of at least:

options.text: 60 kt
100 kt
30 kt
150 kt

explanation: Winds above 60 kt in a narrow band near the tropopause are termed jet streams.

question: For exam purposes, typical jet stream dimensions are taken as:

options.text: About 20 000 nm long, 20 nm wide and 0.2 nm deep
About 2000 nm long, 200 nm wide and 2 nm deep
About 200 nm long, 20 nm wide and 2 nm deep
About 2000 nm long, 2000 nm wide and 20 nm deep

explanation: These give a depth-to-width ratio of 1:100 and width-to-length ratio of 1:10, showing that a jet is a long, flat ribbon.

question: Jet streams are caused by:

options.text: Strong surface heating over hot deserts in summer
Large vertical temperature contrasts within very stable air near the tropopause
Friction as strong winds cross high mountain ranges
Large horizontal temperature contrasts, which produce strong thermal winds

explanation: Where cold and warm air masses lie side by side the thermal wind is large, and the wind increases strongly with height up to the tropopause.

question: The core of a jet stream is normally found:

options.text: Exactly at the level of the 500 hPa surface
In the middle of the stratosphere, near 25 km
Just below the tropopause, often near a break in it
At the surface, along the line of the cold front

explanation: The wind increases with height up to the tropopause, where the temperature contrast reverses, so the maximum is just below the tropopause.

question: Speeds recorded in jet streams have occasionally exceeded:

options.text: 300 kt
600 kt
100 kt

explanation: Jet cores commonly carry 100–200 kt. Over South-East Asia and Japan in winter, speeds above 300 kt have been recorded on rare occasions.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere, looking downstream along a jet stream, the cold air is:

options.text: Directly below the core only
On the right
On the left
Above the core

explanation: The jet blows with cold air (low pressure aloft) on its left in the Northern Hemisphere, like any thermal wind.

question: Clear air turbulence near a jet stream is strongest:

options.text: Exactly in the core, where the wind speed is greatest
Near or just below the core on the cold side, with a secondary area above it
Far below the core, in the friction layer near the surface front
On the warm side, well above the core, where the wind speeds are falling fastest

explanation: The largest vertical and horizontal shears are on the cold side just below the core.

question: Subtropical jet streams are found:

options.text: Along the Equator, near the 500 hPa level, throughout the year
Over the poles in winter, near the 50 hPa level
Along the polar front, near the 700 hPa level
On the poleward side of the subtropical highs, near 200 hPa

explanation: The subtropical jet is a near-permanent feature linked to the Hadley circulation, typically around FL390.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere the subtropical jet is typically found:

options.text: On the Equator in summer and about 25°N in winter
About 5–10°N in all seasons, close to the ITCZ
About 25–40°N in winter, moving to about 40–45°N in summer
About 60–70°N in all seasons, near the Arctic front

explanation: Like other features of the general circulation, it follows the sun, moving poleward in summer and equatorward in winter.

question: The polar front jet stream:

options.text: Lies at the 50 hPa level over the poles in the polar winter
Is a permanent easterly jet over India and Africa in summer
Is found over the Equator at about FL500 throughout the whole year
Lies roughly parallel to the surface fronts of polar front depressions

explanation: The polar front jet is linked to the temperature contrast at the polar front and is found above and on the cold side of the surface fronts, typically around 300 hPa.

question: Compared with the subtropical jet, the polar front jet is:

options.text: Lower, more variable in position and linked to the surface fronts
Higher, more permanent and linked to the subtropical highs rather than fronts
Always easterly, unlike the westerly subtropical jet
Found only in summer, when the polar front is most active

explanation: The polar front jet is typically near 300 hPa and moves with the depressions, while the subtropical jet is higher (200 hPa) and more persistent.

question: In winter, the Northern Hemisphere polar front jet compared with its summer state is:

options.text: Further north and stronger, as the polar air is colder
Further south and stronger, as the temperature contrast is greater
Further north and weaker, as the temperature contrast is smaller
Further south and weaker, as the tropical air is cooler

explanation: In winter the polar front moves towards lower latitudes and the contrast between polar and tropical air increases, strengthening the jet.

question: The tropical (equatorial) easterly jet occurs:

options.text: In the northern summer, about 10–20°N, from the South China Sea across India to Africa
In the northern winter, over central Europe and the Mediterranean, near 300 hPa
Throughout the year, directly over the Equator, near the 500 hPa level
In the polar winter, over the Arctic, near the 50 hPa level

explanation: Intense heating of the Asian landmass in summer reverses the usual temperature gradient aloft, producing a strong easterly current at high level over southern Asia and Africa.

question: The tropical easterly jet is easterly, unlike most jet streams, because:

options.text: It is driven directly by the easterly trade winds at the surface
Heated Asian land makes the air to the north warmer, reversing the gradient
The Coriolis force reverses its direction close to the Equator
It lies in the Southern Hemisphere, where winds turn the other way

explanation: With the warm air poleward and cooler air equatorward, the thermal wind becomes easterly.

question: The polar night jet is found:

options.text: In the trade wind belt at the surface, all year
At low level along the polar front in spring
In summer, at the tropopause directly over the Equator and the tropics
In winter, high in the stratosphere near 50 hPa, in higher latitudes

explanation: During the polar winter the stratosphere over the pole becomes very cold, and a strong westerly jet forms high in the stratosphere.

question: The Arctic jet stream:

options.text: An easterly jet over Africa during the summer monsoon
A permanent jet over the Equator near the 100 hPa level, blowing all year
A winter jet between Arctic and polar air, with its core near 400 hPa
A summer jet found only above 100 hPa near the pole

explanation: The Arctic jet is a transient winter feature, associated with outbreaks of Arctic air over North America and northern Eurasia.

question: The Somali (Findlater) jet is:

options.text: A low-level jet off East Africa in the summer monsoon
The subtropical jet over South America in summer
A polar front jet over Europe in winter
A stratospheric jet over Antarctica in the winter months

explanation: It is an example of a local, low-level jet driven by the summer monsoon flow across the Arabian Sea.

question: In July, the general pattern of upper winds in the Northern Hemisphere has moved, compared with January:

options.text: About 15° further south
About 45° further north
Not at all
About 15° further north

explanation: Most features of the general circulation shift poleward in summer and equatorward in winter, by roughly 15° of latitude.

question: From the ground, a jet stream may be recognised by:

options.text: Towering cumulus building over the hills in the afternoon
A sheet of stratus covering the hilltops all day
Fast-moving streaks of cirrus, often at an angle to the lower cloud
Fog banks drifting slowly along the coast in the early morning

explanation: High-level cirrus streaks in the jet move rapidly and often cross the direction of the lower cloud.

question: In flight, signs that an aircraft is near a jet stream include:

options.text: A steady decrease in wind speed and very smooth air at cruise level
Rapid changes in temperature and drift, rising wind speed, and CAT
Moderate icing and frequent lightning at cruise level
A steady rise in the surface pressure below the aircraft

explanation: Crossing the jet's frontal zone brings temperature changes, large drift changes and often turbulence.

question: On which chart are jet streams shown with their position, level and maximum speed?

options.text: The aerodrome forecast
The surface analysis chart for the time of departure
The significant weather chart
The METAR summary

explanation: Significant weather charts show jet axes with arrows, the flight level of the core and the maximum speed. Upper wind charts also show them.

question: When crossing a jet stream that is causing turbulence, a pilot should consider:

options.text: Climbing into the core, where the wind is strongest and the air smoothest
Flying along the cold side just below the core, where the shear is greatest
Increasing speed to the maximum operating speed to cross it quickly
Changing level away from the cold side below the core, at penetration speed

explanation: The worst turbulence is just below the core on the cold side. A level change of a few thousand feet often reduces it.

question: An aircraft at FL350 in the Northern Hemisphere experiences a strong westerly wind and finds the temperature getting colder as it turns left (north) out of the jet. This is consistent with:

options.text: Moving towards the cold side of the jet
Moving towards the warm side of the jet
Moving into the core of the jet
Moving into the subtropical high

explanation: With the westerly jet, cold air lies to the north (on the left facing downstream). Moving north brings the aircraft into colder air on the cold side.

question: In the Southern Hemisphere, upper westerlies blow with the cold air:

options.text: To the north of the jet
On the right when looking downstream
Above the jet core
On the left when looking downstream

explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere the pole is to the south, and with your back to a westerly wind the south is on the right.

question: Jet streams generally move:

options.text: Eastward in summer and westward in winter, with the seasons
Poleward in summer and equatorward in winter, following the sun
Not at all, as their positions are fixed by the continents
Equatorward in summer and poleward in winter, against the sun

explanation: Both subtropical and polar front jets shift with the heat equator and the polar front.

question: Forecasts of jet streams are produced mainly from:

options.text: Radiosonde data and numerical models, confirmed by aircraft reports
Satellite cloud pictures alone, without any upper-air data
Barograph traces from a network of surface stations
Surface wind observations from coastal stations, used alone without upper-air data

explanation: Upper-air soundings give the wind and temperature fields from which contour charts and jet positions are derived. Aircraft reports are a vital supplement over oceans and deserts.

question: An aircraft heading east at FL350 in the Northern Hemisphere is in a jet stream with cold air to the north. To reduce the headwind on a westbound return flight, it would be best to:

options.text: Climb into the stratosphere where the wind always reverses to easterly
Stay exactly in the core, where the wind is steadiest
Descend to just below the core on the cold side
Move away from the core, either laterally or vertically, rather than stay in it

explanation: A westbound aircraft is fighting the westerly jet. Winds decrease away from the core, so changing level or track to leave it reduces the headwind; just below the core on the cold side is also where turbulence is worst.

question: Over a Northern Hemisphere polar front depression, the upper wind ahead of the warm front at jet level is typically:

options.text: South-easterly
North-easterly
North-westerly
South-westerly

explanation: The jet follows the frontal zone; ahead of the warm front it blows from the north-west on the forward side of the upper trough.

question: Behind the cold front of a Northern Hemisphere polar front depression, the jet stream is typically:

options.text: North-westerly
South-westerly
Easterly
Northerly

explanation: The jet runs parallel to the cold front, with the cold air on its left (north-west).

question: The 1000–500 hPa thickness lines run east–west, decreasing northwards. In the Northern Hemisphere, the thermal wind for this layer is:

options.text: Southerly
Northerly
Westerly
Easterly

explanation: The thermal wind blows parallel to the thickness lines with low thickness (cold air) on the left.

question: The surface wind is northerly, and the thermal wind is westerly. With increasing height in the Northern Hemisphere, the wind will:

options.text: Back towards north-westerly and then westerly
Become calm
Veer towards north-easterly and then easterly
Stay northerly

explanation: Adding a westerly component to a northerly wind turns it anticlockwise (backs) towards north-west and, higher up, west. Backing with height indicates cold advection.

question: The jet streams of the Southern Hemisphere, compared with the Northern Hemisphere, are generally:

options.text: Much stronger than any jet found in the Northern Hemisphere
Absent in winter, when the temperature contrast disappears
Mostly easterly, because the Coriolis force is reversed
More constant in position, with the polar front jet around 50°S

explanation: The largely oceanic Southern Hemisphere has fewer disturbances from land masses.

question: An upper ridge on a 300 hPa chart is shown by:

options.text: Straight east–west contours with even spacing
Contours bulging towards the pole, with higher values
A closed contour of low values at the centre
Contours bulging towards the Equator, with lower values

explanation: An upper ridge extends high contour values poleward; an upper trough extends low values equatorward.
